stories.headline: Glacial collapse triggered Nepal flash floods, not earthquake: USGS
stories.title: Glacial collapse triggered Nepal flash floods, not earthquake: USGS
stories.summary: Washington, Aug 27: The Nepal flash floods were triggered by a glacial collapse and not by a 4.4 magnitude earthquake as reported earlier, the US Geological Survey (USGS) said. The USGS said additional analysis of the long-period seismic waves indicated that the tremors were generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow. The flash floods originating in Tibet on Wednesday left a trail of death and destruction in Rasuwa and Dhading districts of Nepal, killing 162 people and leaving 750, including 133 Indian nationals, missing. “This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred,” the USGS said in an update to its note on the event. It also upgraded the magnitude of the seismic event to 5.2 from the 4.4 assessed earlier. “The USGS determined that the seismic event was a glacial collapse and debris flow that caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream,” it said. Daniel Shugar, an Associate Professor of geomorphology at the University of Calgary in Canada said the flash floods were triggered by a glacier that rolled off a cliff at 5,200 meters. Shugar compared the satellite images of the region taken on Wednesday and Tuesday, a day before the natural disaster struck Nepal. “Comparing satellite imagery from yesterday and today, the glaciers in the vicinity do seem to have lost a fair bit of snow in the last 24 hours,” Shugar was quoted as saying by the New Scientist magazine. “My guess is that snow melt, and glacier ice melt as well, injected a lot of liquid water into the glacier, which percolated down to the bed and lubricated it. That was enough for it to collapse,” he said.

NDRF inspector general Narendra Singh Bundela said the situation was being continuously monitored in coordination with both state governments and other agencies.
Twenty NDRF teams have been positioned across the two states to undertake evacuation, rescue and relief operations if flooding or waterlogging occurs.
Nine teams are deployed in Bihar and 11 in Uttar Pradesh, including one in Kushinagar district near Gorakhpur.
The Central Water Commission is also closely tracking water levels and providing regular updates, Bundela said.
Authorities are monitoring the Gandak River at Valmikinagar in Bihar’s West Champaran district, where the first barrage on the Indian side of the Nepal border is located.
No impact from the Nepal floods has been observed there so far, according to the NDRF official.

Four additional NDRF teams are on standby in Ghaziabad for possible deployment in the neighbouring country.

stories.headline: India sends second flight with 37.5 tonnes of aid to flood-hit Nepal
stories.title: India sends second flight with 37.5 tonnes of aid to flood-hit Nepal
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 27 : India on Thursday dispatched a second flight carrying 37.5 tonnes of humanitarian supplies, medicines, and food packets to support Nepal's relief efforts after devastating flash floods that have left over 160 dead and hundreds missing. External Affairs Minister (EAM) S. Jaishankar took to X and reaffirmed India's commitment to supporting Nepal in the rescue and relief operations. "A second flight has just taken off, carrying 37.5 tonnes of HADR material, medicines & food packets for Nepal," EAM Jaishankar said in a post on X. "India remains in close and continuous touch with the Nepalese authorities. We will continue to strongly support the ongoing relief efforts," he added. According to the latest official update, the bodies of 162 people swept away by a massive flash flood in Nepal's Bhote Koshi River have been recovered as of Thursday morning. The remains were recovered from riverbanks in several downstream districts along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahu, Nawalparasi (East) and Nawalparasi West, the Police said in a notice. The aid follows a first 10-tonne shipment sent on Wednesday. India's Ambassador to Nepal, Naveen Srivastava, formally handed over the aid consignment to Nepal's Minister of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, Khadak Raj Paudel. The assistance includes essential relief materials to help communities affected by widespread flooding and landslides. Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India stands firmly with Nepal and remains committed to extending all possible support. The floods in Nepal, triggered by heavy monsoon rains, have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, homes and agricultural land, displacing thousands of families. Rescue and relief operations are ongoing across several provinces, with local authorities struggling to cope with the scale of the disaster. India's assistance comes as part of its longstanding policy of 'Neighbourhood First', under which New Delhi has consistently provided humanitarian aid to neighbouring countries during emergencies. --IANS

article_sentences: Expressing deep anguish over the severe flooding and flash floods in Nepal, All India Congress Committee (AICC) President and Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday (August 27, 2026) urged the Union Government to step in immediately to assist stranded tourists and pilgrims from India, including those from Karnataka.

Speaking to media representatives at the Kalaburagi Airport, the veteran leader said that he would write a formal letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi seeking his intervention for comprehensive compensation and assistance measures for affected families.
Mr. Kharge noted that the catastrophic deluge in Nepal has affected numerous citizens from across the country, with hundreds caught in the deluge, several lives lost, and many reported missing.
He extended his heartfelt condolences to the families of those who died in the natural calamity.

Emphasising the close bilateral relations between the two nations, Mr. Kharge urged the Indian government to extend substantial relief aid to Nepal to support search, rescue, and rehabilitation efforts alongside the foreign administration.

He clarified that decisions concerning ministerial appointments, portfolio reallocations, or cabinet changes fall strictly under the purview of the party’s central leadership.
“Any inclusion to or removal from the cabinet will have to be done with my consultation.
I have received no proposal on the matter,” he said.

stories.summary: The Karnataka government has decided to declare 101 taluks drought-hit, while another 32 that have met the initial eligibility criteria are being reassessed, Deputy Chief Minister and Revenue Minister G Parameshwara said on Thursday.

article_sentences: The Karnataka government has decided to declare 101 taluks drought-hit, while another 32 that have met the initial eligibility criteria are being reassessed, Deputy Chief Minister and Revenue Minister G Parameshwara said on Thursday.
Addressing a press conference at Vidhana Soudha, Parameshwara described the current conditions as unprecedented and said the government was spending Rs 635 crore on drought management.
He maintained that there was no shortage of funds to protect residents and livestock from the impact of the rainfall deficit.
Karnataka received 465 mm of rain between 1 June and 26 August against the normal 666 mm, resulting in a deficit of 30 per cent.
Twenty-nine districts and 190 taluks have recorded deficient to large-deficient rainfall, while 12 taluks are experiencing a severe shortfall.
As of 26 August, 134 taluks had witnessed dry spells lasting more than three consecutive weeks, making them eligible for an assessment under Trigger-1 of the Centre’s Drought Manual, 2020.
The state subsequently carried out ground verification using the prescribed assessment parameters and found 101 taluks eligible to be declared drought-hit.
Another 32 taluks that qualified under Trigger-1 are being reassessed.
The conditions in the 101 taluks will be reviewed every 15 days after the formal declaration.
Similar verification has been conducted at the hobli level, and the data is being examined.
Under the drought manual, Trigger-1 applies to areas experiencing dry spells of at least three consecutive weeks.
Trigger-2 assesses sowing coverage, crop health, soil moisture, groundwater levels and water availability in tanks and reservoirs.

stories.headline: Tata Power's $640-Million Singapore Problem
stories.title: Tata Power's $640-Million Singapore Problem
stories.summary: India's largest integrated private power utility has run out of road in Singapore's courts, at least for now. On August 26, 2026, the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC) dismissed every application Tata Power had filed to overturn a $490.32 million arbitration award won by Kleros Capital Partners, a UK-based investment firm. The court rejected both of Tata Power's core arguments: that the tribunal's damages calculation (quantum) was wrong, and that the majority's decision-making process had breached natural justice. With interest accruing since November 2020 and legal costs added on, the total bill has now crossed $640 million, or upwards of ₹6,000 crore. Tata Power's shares fell as much as 5% in the following session, and the company has confirmed it will appeal to the Singapore Court of Appeal. The market cap loss from today's fall roughly matches the full quantum of the firm' liabilities from the award, indicating how quickly the market has priced in the liability and the uncertainty linked to it. How the dispute began The roots of the case go back to a coal partnership in Russia that never materialised. Kleros initiated arbitration proceedings against Tata Power at the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) in November 2020, alleging that Tata Power had breached confidentiality and non-circumvention obligations tied to a proposed joint pursuit of the Krutogorovo coal project in Russia. A three-member tribunal — Professor Lawrence Boo (presiding), Stuart Isaacs KC, and retired Indian Supreme Court judge Amal K. Ganguli heard the matter. In September 2023, the panel unanimously found Tata Power liable, concluding that the company had misused confidential information, deliberately circumvented Kleros, made misleading statements, and concealed material facts in order to pursue the project on its own account. Liability was never in question after that point, only the size of the damages. In July 2025, the tribunal issued its award on quantum. Here the panel split 2:1: Boo and Isaacs, in the majority, awarded Kleros $490.32 million plus simple interest of 5.33% per annum from November 30, 2020, until payment. All three arbitrators agreed Tata Power owed something; they differed only on methodology and amount. Rather than resisting enforcement, Tata Power took the award to the Singapore courts directly, challenging both the quantum and the fairness of the tribunal's process. That challenge is what the SICC dismissed on August 26. What happens next Tata Power has said it will file an appeal with the Singapore Court of Appeal within the mandatory 28-day window from the SICC's order. But this is a narrower and steeper climb than the challenge just rejected. Appellate review of arbitration-related court decisions is deliberately constrained. International arbitration is designed around finality, and courts at the seat of arbitration (Singapore, in this case) generally give tribunals wide deference on quantum and process once liability has been unanimously established. The more immediate complication: filing an appeal does not automatically pause enforcement. Unless Tata Power secures an explicit stay from the Singapore courts, Kleros is free to pursue enforcement of the award in Singapore or in other jurisdictions where Tata Power or its group entities hold assets while the appeal plays out. That makes the coming weeks less about the legal argument and more about interim relief: whether Tata Power can buy itself time without the liability crystallising into an immediate cash call. Does this set a precedent? The SICC's order turns on the specific facts of this arbitration rather than announcing a broad legal principle. But it is a useful data point for Indian companies increasingly exposed to international commercial arbitration on cross-border deal conduct, not just contract non-performance. Two things stand out. First, allegations around confidentiality, circumvention, and misuse of shared information are treated seriously by arbitral tribunals and are hard to unwind on appeal once liability is unanimous. Second, seat courts like Singapore's, much like London's or Hong Kong's set a high bar for "natural justice" and "quantum" challenges, making them a weak lever once an award has been issued by a properly constituted panel. The market's verdict: a bigger hit than the award itself Tata Power's market capitalisation stood at roughly ₹1,19,346 crore on August 25, just before the ruling. By August 27, with shares down as much as 5% intraday before settling closer to a 4–4.3% decline, market cap had fallen to around ₹1,12,220 crore — a loss of close to ₹6,000–7,000 crore (roughly $700–800 million) in investor wealth in a single session. That one-day loss is, notably, larger than the original $490 million principal award (about ₹4,300 crore) and comparable in size to the full $640 million liability including interest and costs. In other words, the market moved to price in something close to the worst-case cash impact almost immediately, rather than waiting for clarity on provisioning or the appeal's outcome. The reaction also has to be read against where the stock already was. Tata Power shares were trading near ₹349–364 post-ruling, well off their 52-week high of ₹464.9 hit in April 2026 and closer to the 52-week low of ₹342.5. With the firm's renewables, manufacturing, and transmission growth story all strong, the stock was priced for a lot to go right if this ruling had gone in its favour. Cash, debt, and the provisioning question On paper, Tata Power's ₹12,831 crore cash pile could cover the roughly ₹6,000 crore liability outright. In practice, doing so would meaningfully dent the liquidity buffer at a moment when operating cash flow is already negative and capital expenditure is running at record levels to fund the company's renewables and manufacturing build-out. The more pressing issue is accounting, not liquidity. Tata Power had not recognised any provision for the Kleros award in its FY26 financial statements, choosing to rely on legal advice while the challenge was pending. That position becomes difficult to defend now that a court has confirmed the award is "final and binding" and payable immediately — accounting standards generally require a provision once an obligation is probable and reliably estimable, and an unappealed, court-confirmed arbitral award is about as unambiguous a trigger as exists. Analysts are likely to press management on provisioning treatment at the next results call. Tata Power's likely paths forward ● Appeal and seek a stay of enforcement — buys time but is unlikely to prevent auditors from forcing a provision given the SICC's language. ● Negotiate a settlement with Kleros — common once appeal odds look weak; could involve a discount for early or certain payment versus continued litigation. ● Fund payment from the balance sheet — feasible given the ₹12,831 crore cash position, but would tighten liquidity headroom already under pressure from negative operating cash flow and record capex. ● Raise fresh debt, or draw on Tata Sons/group support — plausible given the group's scale, though it adds to a net debt load already up sharply quarter-on-quarter. ● Monetise assets — stake sales in renewable SPVs or InvIT-style structures, a route Tata Power has used before to manage leverage, could generate a one-off cash pool without touching core operations. The bottom line This is a genuine capital-allocation event for Tata Power. Against a quarter that delivered ₹1,401 crore in consolidated PAT but negative operating cash flow, a $640 million liability is large enough to influence financing plans, credit metrics, and possibly the pace of renewable capex the market has been rewarding the stock for. Expect provisioning treatment, the appeal's progress, and the funding source for eventual payment to dominate investor questions through the rest of FY27.

stories.headline: AI can augment reasoning but cannot substitute judicial conscience: CJI Surya Kant
stories.title: AI can augment reasoning but cannot substitute judicial conscience: CJI Surya Kant
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 27: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Wednesday said the judiciary’s governing principle is that artificial intelligence may augment judicial reasoning, but it cannot substitute judicial conscience, and that a permanent apex body has been proposed to supervise the adoption and accountability of the new technology. Speaking at a bilateral meeting with Ulrich Herrmann, the presiding judge of the Federal Court of Justice at Karlsruhe in Germany, CJI Kant said that artificial intelligence (AI) is being used in certain defined support functions such as legal research, judgement translation into 16 languages and as a conversational interface for citizens to look for case status and procedures. He said that while these tools are designed to reduce repetitive work, they do not determine judicial outcomes. “Artificial intelligence may augment judicial reasoning, but it cannot substitute judicial conscience. Draft regulations from the Supreme Court's AI Committee permit administrative uses such as scheduling, transcription and translation, while barring AI from assessing witness credibility, flight risk, recidivism or bail eligibility; a permanent apex body has been proposed to supervise the adoption and accountability of AI,” he said. “Our two judiciaries share the same underlying responsibility: to preserve judicial independence and public confidence while adapting our institutions to new forms of litigation and new expectations of access. “Technology and administrative reform can support this responsibility, but neither can replace careful adjudication, human judgment and fidelity to law,” he said. The CJI said that institutional mediation centres, Lok Adalats and digital Lok Adalats, including the Supreme Court's recent special Lok Adalat, ‘Samadhan Samaroh’, have brought settlement within reach of parties well beyond major cities, supported by trained professionals, case managers and secure digital systems. “As two major trading partners, our judiciaries and mediation institutions stand to gain from exchanging experience on cross-border commercial mediation, the recognition and enforcement of mediated settlements, and joint training for mediators handling India-Germany commercial disputes,” he said. At the outset, the CJI said that both the countries have developed different judicial structures and legal traditions, as India follows a common-law tradition with one integrated judicial hierarchy, while Germany has a civil-law system with separate branches of federal jurisdiction. “These differences make the exchange particularly useful. They allow us to compare how our institutions deal with the same practical concerns, including appellate workload, consistency of case law, timely disposal, judicial administration and access to justice,” he said. The CJI said he is approaching the meeting with three themes that speak directly to the challenges the two judiciaries share, such as harnessing technology and AI in the administration of justice, strengthening cross-border mediation and other dispute resolution mechanisms, and deepening institutional cooperation through an MoU. “I also see considerable value in identifying areas in which our courts, judges, registries and judicial academies can continue this engagement through a structured and reciprocal programme,” he said. The CJI said he sees value in anchoring any MoU in the themes already discussed: technology and AI in court administration, and cross-border mediation and dispute resolution, alongside the commercial and business law focus and the digitalisation of judicial processes that the Hanseatic court's concept note already identifies as priorities. “I propose that each side identify one institutional point of contact so that today's discussion can be converted into a workable programme, with the MoU or another suitable arrangement to follow once the appropriate authorities on both sides have considered its scope, frequency, participants, confidentiality requirements and working language,” he said. Giving an overview of the Indian judiciary, the CJI said that unlike Germany, India has no separate constitutional court. “The Supreme Court is simultaneously the final appellate court in civil and criminal matters and the country's highest constitutional court, with original jurisdiction under Article 32 to enforce fundamental rights,” he said. The CJI also said that India’s approach has been to make courts not merely more technological, but more accessible, transparent and responsive for every stakeholder in the justice delivery system. On the shared institutional challenge, CJI Kant said Germany's electronic case files, the e-Justice council, the Bund-Laender Commission and the proposed Federal Justice Cloud reflect a similar commitment to a secure digital foundation for justice delivery. “Both our judiciaries agree that judicial decisions must remain with judges and legally authorised judicial officers, whatever the degree of digital transformation,” he said. Promoting mediation as another mode of dispute resolution has always been at the top of the priority list of the Chief Justice of India, right from day one, CJI Kant said. The CJI is on a four-day visit to Germany and the UK during which he will address several programmes.

stories.headline: J&K Deputy CM says Congress likely to join government soon, attacks BJP over ‘discrimination’ against Jammu
stories.title: J&K Deputy CM says Congress likely to join government soon, attacks BJP over ‘discrimination’ against Jammu
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 27: Jammu and Kashmir Deputy Chief Minister Surinder Choudhary said on Thursday that the Congress is expected to join the National Conference-led government soon, describing the move as a natural development given the two parties’ alliance. Choudhary said the National Conference had wanted Congress to become part of the government since the alliance was formed, but that the final decision had rested with the Congress. “As far as Congress is concerned, ever since this government was formed, when we entered into the alliance, it was our desire and we wanted Congress to join,” he said. “But Congress was unable to take a decision. Now Congress is taking a decision, and I think everyone should be happy because it is an alliance partner.” He said Congress joining the government would strengthen the administration and help it deliver for the people. “If Congress also comes in, the government will run with greater strength and we will be able to work for the people,” Choudhary said. “Because it is our alliance partner, they have a right to come into the government.” Asked what the National Conference was offering Congress, including the number of ministerial berths, Choudhary rejected the suggestion that the party was negotiating through inducements. “We are not BJP people. We are not like the BJP people who do horse-trading,” he said. “These are relationships of the heart. We are people who connect hearts, and decisions taken from the heart last long and are for the betterment of the people.” He added: “It does not happen that we will bring someone by giving them greed or temptation. This is the work of the BJP.” Deputy CM attacks BJP over Jammu ‘discrimination’ Choudhary also launched a broadside against the BJP, accusing it of failing to address what he described as discrimination against Jammu. Responding to BJP claims that a cabinet reshuffle could bring down the government, he said the BJP should focus instead on issues affecting the region. He questioned why, according to him, there was no Jammu-based professor serving as vice-chancellor at any of Jammu’s universities and why no local doctor had become director of AIIMS. “Is this not discrimination that professors and doctors from Jammu do not have the right to become vice-chancellors or directors?” he asked. “Are our professors so incompetent? Are our doctors so incompetent that they cannot become vice-chancellors? Can they not become directors of AIIMS, IIM or IIT?” He urged the media in Jammu to question the BJP on these issues rather than focus on the National Conference. “Tell them not to talk about things here and there. Tell them why discrimination against Jammu is still not ending,” he said. Choudhary also alleged that Jammu’s business sector was suffering and challenged the BJP to explain how it planned to revive trade and industry in the region. He referred to the ₹28,000-crore industrial package for Jammu and Kashmir and questioned whether existing industries in Jammu had benefited from it. “Go to the Gangyal Industrial Estate, go to Bari Brahmana Industrial Estate, go to Samba, go to Kathua and wherever our industrial estates are,” he said. “Ask whether the old industries of Jammu and Kashmir have received anything from the package. Nothing has been given.” Power tariffs, inflation and cost of living The Deputy Chief Minister also defended the government on electricity tariffs, arguing that the issue should be viewed against the record of the previous BJP-PDP administration. “You should compare the last 12 years,” he said. “Find out how much electricity rates increased during the BJP period and how high electricity bills were.” He also pointed to the government’s electricity amnesty measures and challenged the BJP to answer questions about the rising prices of basic commodities. “Ask the BJP people how much sugar costs. Is it ₹70 or ₹75 a kilo?” he said. “Ask them how much pulses cost. Ask them the price of vegetables and onions.” Choudhary said the impact of inflation was particularly severe on ordinary households. “For a poor man who has only one bulb, what does he know whether the bill is bigger or smaller?” he said. “He knows the price of the sugar he needs for his tea.” He also accused the BJP of failing to address rising education and healthcare costs. “Ask them why fees in universities have increased,” he said. “Ask them about the fees in hospitals. These are important issues.” ‘We will take back Article 370 and statehood’ On Article 370 and statehood, Choudhary said the National Conference remained committed to restoring Jammu and Kashmir’s special status and statehood. “We will take back 370. article_sentences: The Supreme Court recently stayed the order passed by the Bar Council of India permanently debarring Madhya Pradesh-based advocate and former judicial officer, Narendra Kumar Jain, from practising law over his alleged unwarranted remarks on the judiciary.

A bench comprising Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta stayed the BCI's order, which had found him guilty of professional misconduct over allegations of making remarks against the judiciary and judges.
The bench also issued notice to the BCI on Jain's appeal.
Challenging the BCI's order, the petitioner, in his plea, claimed that he was not given an opportunity to defend himself, violating the principles of natural justice.
Senior Advocate Vivek Tankha appeared for the former judicial officer, and based on his submissions, the bench stayed the BCI's order.

article_sentences: From India and Canada to Iran and Venezuela, the countries may be thousands of miles apart and have little in common economically.

Yet they have found themselves facing the same problem: an unpredictable US trade policy under President Donald Trump, in which tariffs and sanctions are being deployed for reasons that go beyond conventional trade disputes.

Trade deficits remain a key justification for many measures, but Trump has increasingly tied economic pressure to wars, Russian oil, fentanyl, immigration, deportations, drug trafficking, nuclear programmes and even the domestic policies of US allies.

That sequence of threaten, negotiate, delay, collapse talks, retaliate and threaten further escalation has become a defining feature of Trump's approach, making the tariff regime difficult for governments and businesses to predict.
Canada has emerged as one of the clearest and most recently escalated examples of how Trump's trade policy has expanded beyond trade.

In the latest, Ottawa announced 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 50 per cent retaliatory tariffs on C$27.6 billion of US goods, effective September 8, matching Washington's measures “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.”
The tariffs cover steel, dairy, seafood, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics and other goods.
Canada also announced a C$7.5 billion support package for affected workers and businesses.
The move followed Trump's 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods after trade talks collapsed.
But the dispute has long involved more than trade.
In 2025, Trump repeatedly cited fentanyl trafficking and illegal immigration, accusing Ottawa of failing to secure the northern border, while also alleging discriminatory treatment of US products.
The negotiations brought in another non-trade issue.
